paragraphs.text: Explanation of the Birth in the Flesh of Christ our Lord.
By the power of our Lord Jesus Christ we begin to write the book of the Explanations composed by the teacher who feared God, Mar Thomas of Edessa, and by Mar Cyrus, his fellow worker.
The first, composed by Mar Thomas:
On the birth in the flesh of Christ our Lord.
First chapter: to the one who asked him to set it down in writing.
Second: what the chapters of the Explanation are.
Third: an inquiry into why we celebrate this feast.
Fourth: what the benefits are that were given to us through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Fifth: why these benefits were not revealed until now.
Sixth: that there had to be the mediation of something through which we might receive these benefits from God.
Seventh: for these reasons God took nothing else at this time for his revelation except an ordinary human being, Christ our Lord.
Ninth: why our Lord's humanity was not taken from the earth, but from a virgin, without union with a man.
Tenth: why God arranged for our Lord's humanity to be conceived in the season of Nisan.
Eleventh: an exhortation to good conduct.

First Chapter: To the one who asked him to set it down in writing.

Your excellent counsel, which you share with the brothers called to our community, and the command you laid on me together with them, O chosen of God, Mar Moses the instructor, have stirred troubling thoughts in me and thrown me into shifting reflections. For you commanded me to complete in writing as well the "Cause" that I delivered after our holy master Mar Aba the Interpreter, on the glorious nativity of our Lord and Savior Christ. I am afraid to do this. I fear that, since it is not perfect, it may be judged wholly contemptible by those who love to find fault with cause and without cause. Yet I also fear failing to carry out the command [?], as a timid servant who does not transgress a command or slight your counsel, should anyone dispute it, since all that you say aims at the fear of the living God. But while I was turning over these thoughts and others like them, I judged it right to satisfy your wish and leave others to say what they please. I should not fear envious words, which count for nothing with God, and so give you, who are fair in Christ's sight through good will and perfect conduct, cause to complain against me for not obeying your command. So, asking for the help of your prayers, which are acceptable to Christ, here I give myself to fulfilling your wish. Before all else I ask this of you, and of all who may in any way come upon these writings: do not blame me in any respect, as though I had supposed I was able to complete everything our master said on this subject exactly as he said it, and therefore ventured to speak it aloud or to put it in writing. Rather, let this be assumed about my words, as I am myself convinced: all of mine, compared with our master's, can be compared to his only as an image to its archetype, or as a shadow to the body from which it arises. Just as it is not fitting for a small lamp to shine where the rays of the sun are spread, so too my words fade away when our master's shine with the rays of their understanding. I therefore set out first the headings along which the whole Cause runs, for the reader's greater benefit, and then I begin to say what the order of each of them requires in the matter of the Cause. For your wisdom and understanding know that those who are about to travel a road of many miles, which they do not expect to cover all at once, are greatly helped by receiving signs and markers along the way before they set out to walk. If they keep these in mind, they can travel without straying, from sign to sign and from marker to marker, until they reach the end of the road. If this is so, it is plain that it is even more useful for those who wish to take in a discourse of many words to learn first of all what the headings of the subject are. For if they do this, then when they are required to speak, even if they cannot recite the writings so as to recall the whole discourse, they can still speak with ease, because they have already learned the number and content of all the headings, even if they fall short in the discourse that lies between them.

Second Chapter: What the headings of the Cause are.

It is clear to everyone that this feast which we celebrate today is the nativity of Christ. Yet the mind does not rest content with learning only this, that the feast is our Lord's nativity. It goes on to ask several questions, beginning with why we celebrate it. When we examine this and find that it is because of the great benefits given to us through our Lord Christ, who was born today for all creation, and that we celebrate so that his benefits may be made firm in us as we call them to mind and fulfill the will of their Giver, we are then required to say what these benefits are. After we have recounted and shown them, we are asked why benefits so surpassing all others came only now [?], such that we even take delight in them. Another question follows: without the mediation of something, these benefits could not have reached us from God [?]. When we have shown this too, that there had to be something through which they could be received, it is asked why they were revealed through nothing else but a man. When we have shown the many things that required the assumption of a man from among us, another question arises: if a man was needed for these reasons, then he alone should have sufficed for our salvation. So we make known that the dispensation also required God to be in him, so that it might be known that an ordinary man could not save us. Nor could we have received the benefits bestowed on us from God without the mediation of something. Since it appears that we celebrate the feast of his nativity today because of the benefits given to us through our Lord Christ, the benefits are shown for what they are, and the hearer is also set at ease about why they were not revealed before this time [?]. It appears too that their revelation required the mediation of something, and that this could be nothing other than a man. Yet he was not an ordinary man, but one in whom God was able to do all things. Then come the questions about what he did in his dispensation for our salvation: why God did not take this man from the earth, as he did the first Adam, or why he had to be born of a woman, and why he was born of a virgin without male seed. After the reason for this has been shown, it remains to ask why God arranged for him to be conceived in the season of Nisan, and what we learn from his being born at this time. After these things we bring the whole Cause to completion, adding a little admonition, which is fitting for the strengthening and correction of the hearers.

Third Chapter: An examination of why we celebrate this feast of the holy Nativity.

It is clear that this feast which we celebrate today, and which the holy Church observes in every region with great joy, is the nativity of Christ our Lord. Everyone with the gift of speech proclaims it alike, men and women, from children to the old. But this is asked: do we celebrate this feast today and keep it with such fervor perhaps because of the novelty of the manner of his birth, which took place without union, as we marvel at the power that formed him from the Virgin Mary without male seed? It is indeed known to be a great and exalted wonder that a virgin should give birth without union with a man. But however exalted in power it may be, it would not have been enough on its own, without the other things that are about to be said, to make it the cause of this feast in every region. For we see other exalted wonders that were worked in people's coming into being. Yet because nothing further came of them beyond the manner of their formation, their births are not celebrated with feasts, and rightly so. Such were the births of Adam, of Eve, of Isaac, and of others like them. Each of these is even more worthy of wonder than the next, and each proclaims the divine power greatly.

Let us look first at Isaac's: how great a thing it is that a son should come from a barren and aged woman! Either one of these conditions on its own would have been enough to keep nature from bearing fruit, let alone both together, old age and barrenness at once. Yet this birth did come from seed. But what can seed do in barrenness and old age? Suppose someone sowed one kind of seed on a rock, or threw it into a fiery furnace, or hung it in water or in the air, and it bore fruit in any of these places. That would be a great wonder. In the same way, even if a man were to sow seed ten thousand times in old age and barrenness, it would be a great wonder for a son to come of it, even where only one of these conditions was present. How much more here, where both were found in Sarah! With the blessed Mary, then, one thing was lacking from the order of nature: that she should receive seed. With Sarah, as I said, two things were lacking: youth and fertility, for she was old and barren. And it is easier to believe that the earth brings forth without being sown than that grains falling into a fiery furnace should yield fruit. Of course, to God the hard and the easy are alike. We possess power in measure, so we are not equally able to work with clay and with bronze. For God, however, nothing is harder than anything else, because his power is unbounded, and his nod alone suffices for all things. But judging by our own standard, Isaac's birth is more worthy of wonder than Eve's creation. Eve came not from a womb, nor from nurture, nor from seed, but from a rib taken from a side. And again, the woman came from the man not through a long period of nurture, gradually and by stages. She rose from his sleep in the twinkling of an eye, complete in stature. Adam's creation, in turn, is more wonderful than Eve's. She was a living being formed from a living being, a creature with senses formed from one with senses. But Adam was formed living, rational, and endowed with senses out of the earth, which shares in none of these.

If, then, these too are wonders, each more wonderful than the last, why is it for this birth alone that the Church celebrates such a feast today in every region with all joy? Plainly we do not celebrate this feast merely because we gaze at these outward things [?]. For the Magi too, when they were moved by divine grace in some manner to come and worship him, did not bring offerings that pointed to this. They brought gold, myrrh, and frankincense. The frankincense was a sign that the one who was born is the temple of God, and that in him the Godhead, which is incorporeal, would be worshipped by all rational beings as in an indestructible temple. The gold pointed to his kingship and his commands, and showed that from then on all people ought to receive him and obey him with all their strength. The myrrh made known that by his death he would conquer death and gain a kingdom that can never be shaken in any way. It is clear that they had been made wise by a divine sign in offering him these gifts.

The angel too, when he appeared to the shepherds and brought them the good news, did not glory before them in the fact that our Lord was born of a virgin. What did he say to them? "I bring you good news of great joy, which will be for the whole world." And why? "For today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David." He mentioned the city of David to show that in the one born today the promises God made to the fathers were being fulfilled, and that in him all the nations would be blessed, according to the promises to Abraham: "In your seed all the nations shall be blessed." On this rests, and from it runs on, the promise to David: "From the fruit of your body I will set one on your throne, and of his kingdom there shall be no end." And again: "The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and of his kingdom there shall be no end." He called him Lord because he is Lord of all creatures through his union with God the Word: "For God has made him Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified." He called him Christ because he was set apart and chosen for this, and he is the true Christ. All the earlier ones were anointed with the oil of the Law, but he was anointed by the Holy Spirit: "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." He called him Savior because through him we were to be saved from sin, death, and corruption, and from slavery to Satan. So this is a joy for the whole world: for the nations, who are made worthy of kinship with God, and for the people of Israel, in whom the promises made to their fathers are fulfilled, since all alike are saved from every affliction of this world. It is clear too that the angels share this joy with us, since they also rejoice greatly in our change for the better.

In the same way, the holy Church commemorates John the Baptist every year for this reason: because these things were ministered through him, and because of his perfect and exalted way of life and his death for the fear of God. As we bring all these things of his to mind, we may strive to imitate them as far as we can, so that we may be found worthy to attain with him the delight of the heavenly blessings. We do the same when we commemorate all the holy fathers and those who were martyred for Christ, each in his proper order, for the same purpose I have just stated. So when we celebrate this glorious and honored feast of the nativity of Christ our Lord, we are not looking only at the outward novelty of the manner of his birth, that it took place without union; we will give the reason for that later. We celebrate because of these unspeakable blessings that were given to all creation through Christ our Savior. As we call them to mind and receive teaching about them, we may shape our conduct to the will of their Giver, so that we may be found worthy of the ascent to heaven and of a share in the blessings kept for those who believe rightly and live in keeping with their faith.

Fourth Chapter: What the blessings are that were given to us through our Lord Christ.

What, then, are these blessings that were decreed for us through our Lord Christ, which we gather today to make firm as we celebrate this feast? We must say. We learn them from the holy angels, who cried out with great joy at the time of our Savior's birth: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, and good hope to men." In these three phrases, as if in sections, are set out all the blessings given to us through our Lord Christ.

The holy angels are, as it were, our companions in creation. They saw that we had fallen from the health of the fear of God, been darkened by the black disease of idol worship, become utterly sick in the service of demons, and been weakened by abominable deeds. So they were grieved and indignant, since they could not undertake even one of the things necessary and fitting for our restoration [?]. Indeed, they wished to cut us off as diseased limbs and cast us out of their fellowship. They would have done so, had not God, the good Lord of all, subjected them in hope of our correction and our return to him, as it is written: "For the creation was subjected to futility, not of its own will, but because of the one who subjected it in hope." For they thought their labor on our behalf futile and fruitless, since we, who had been created and blessed in the fear of God, did not persevere. Yet they persevered [?] in the hope of things to come. In their ministry on our behalf, God strengthened in them the hope of our change for the better through the cry of Abel's blood, the translation of Enoch, and the ascension of Elijah. He strengthened it too by never ceasing, at all times and in every generation, to arrange whatever would help toward our salvation and our return to the truth.

So it was fitting that, as the healthy members of creation, who persevered in the health of their Lord's love, grieved over the sick, and longed in hope for better things, they cried out with great joy when God revealed the blessings decreed for all creation through Christ our Lord. They said, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, and good hope to men." Until then, the glory that men owed to God had been withheld from him. Dumb idols were worshipped, and Satan was served. The demons rejoiced and the devils exulted. Men were insolent and worthy of blame, and at the prompting of the Accuser they did every wickedness without a thought, in their inclination toward abominations. But now, through the one born of the seed of David according to the divine promises, God receives back the glory that all owe him. The Most High, Maker and Benefactor of all, is known and exalted above all his creation. Men are gathered from the scattering of idol worship and are reconciled, turning from the service of demons. The devils are put to shame and the Accuser falls. Men stand upright and please their Maker through the knowledge of the truth and through virtuous conduct, and they receive correction for all their former abominations.

Because of all these things, there is "peace on earth." Men turn from worshipping the work of their own hands and worship in exalted fashion God, their Maker and ours. They live according to his will, so that tranquility, peace, and concord reign on the earth. For the Maker was angry with his creatures and held a threat over all men according to their deeds. But now, through the one who was born, he has gained concord and moderation toward them. "We angels too were angry with them, as zealous servants of their Lord and as laborers and servants of their Benefactor. But as they grow in pleasing the Maker of all, so we too warm our love toward them, broaden our eagerness for their benefit, hold them as healthy members, and love them as dear companions."

The peoples too had all been split against one another. One worshipped the sun, another the moon, another the stars, and another something else. Their enmity toward one another shifted along with the changes of those they called gods. Now they all gain harmony and the love of the fear of God, together with the people of Israel, from whom they had also been estranged, cut off from fellowship with God's saints and all his blessings. Like scattered limbs they gather into one body of the fear of God, in love and harmony, and all their former division is dissolved.

Man, too, gains boundless peace with himself. His body is mortal and his soul immortal, and as much as mortal things are opposed to immortal ones, so much is the activity of the body opposed to the soul. The soul is exalted, discerning, and immortal; it receives the knowledge of God and instruction in his commandments, and so it inclines toward the service of virtue. But the body is without reason or discernment and is mortal; it is drawn toward visible things and held fast by love of them. From this comes a struggle within man that gives him no peace with himself. This struggle is ended through our Lord Christ. He makes the body immortal and uproots from it all its inclination toward passing things, and at the same time he grants the soul unchangeableness, so that it may do God's will and please him without hindrance.

This is the whole wealth over which peace reigns. Men turn to their Maker and praise and exalt him alone, as the cause of all good things, and strive to please him with virtuous conduct. Peace reigns between the Maker and his creatures, between us angels and men, between all the peoples with one another and with Israel, and between man and himself. After all these, they look for nothing else except the hope of the heavenly blessings. For there is "good hope to men": confidence has taken hold from now on. It is a good and abundant hope: the uprooting of sin, freedom from the demons and the Accuser, release from death, the abolition of corruption and resurrection from the grave, the gift of immortality, a share in incorruption, the grace of adoption, the ascent to heaven, and enjoyment with all God's saints. All this has been given to us in these heavenly blessings, which do not pass away and are never withdrawn.

These, then, our honored brother, are the blessings given to us by Christ our Lord, which we celebrate this feast today to make firm, as set out in the interpretation of the phrases the angels spoke. What could be better and more exalted for all the nations than to know God their Creator, the cause of all their good things? Clearly nothing. All the good things of this world, even where they are found, do not bring equal profit where there is no fear of God. But where there is fear of God, shown in confession and in deeds, all things visible and comforting are gathered together, even if there should be a little hardship in some respect. This is especially so after our departure from this world. Suppose someone wishes to go to the gate of the royal court, but once he begins his journey he strays from the road and goes out into a desolate wilderness. However many provisions he carries, they run out and are lost, and nothing is left for him but to die without reaching the place he set out for. In the same way, whoever strays from the straight road and from the fear of the true God loses all the provisions of his life, even if he has them. He does not reach the kingdom that comes from God, but falls under God's endless threat. Even if he has works that seem good, he is like someone who digs a well in the ground, goes down as deep as he can, and finds no spring of water. For idols have no power to benefit those who worship them. Such a person does his good works in the name of God, but of one who is not God and merely bears that name.

What profit is there in this? Clearly none. Suppose someone carries a debt he owes to the crown to whoever is its administrator. On his way to deliver it of his own accord, he sees false men in various places who set up one of their number in the guise of a king to make sport before him. He is deceived by them, goes, and throws down before them the money owed to the crown. Is it not true that after a time, by the command of the true king, he is seized and bound, and that what he gave is not credited to him, because it went to one who was merely called king and is not a king? In the same way, whoever takes all the worship and righteous deeds owed to the true God and throws them down before beings that are not gods, but are called by a name not theirs through the work of demons, will not have a single one of them credited to him when he comes to the judgment of God, the Maker of all. He alone is God, and to him alone all creatures owe worship. So everyone who lacks the knowledge of God loses all his joys, even if he has them for a time. His whole labor turns out profitless, and in his works that seem good he is found without profit; in his works that seem good he is found without reward. He falls under an everlasting threat. This is what all the nations were facing before the coming of Christ.

It is clear, too, that although the people of Israel had kinship with God, the coming of Christ our Lord was also a great good for them. They were raised from a childish way of life, and they too were made worthy of the perfect knowledge of the holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, known in unity. Before, they could not tell the difference between one who speaks of a soul or of the sun as one thing while not realizing that the sun has, as it were, heat and ray, and the soul has mind and word. If we rejoice greatly when we wean an infant from milk and bring it to solid food, how much more is it worth rejoicing that the Israelites, together with all the nations, have attained the perfect knowledge of the holy Trinity! They have attained it in their conduct too, for before they were all alike held fast in [?] attachment to earthly things. Though they knew God, they did not hope for the good things that come from him. Like an infant that still clings to the breast at the time of weaning, they clung to earthly things. But our Lord God fixed in his gospel the expectation of things to come, and they despised and scorned all the things of this world.

This too is the chief good, when it goes together with the fear of God. A rational man who is bound in love to these passing possessions is like a tongue or an eye from which someone hangs an earring as if to adorn it. Not only is it no adornment to them; it also keeps each of them from the activity that is useful to itself and to the whole body. He is like a child who is given a small fig and likes it better than precious stones whose value he cannot grasp. There is nothing, then, so good and delightful for men as to know God with perfect knowledge, to be eager for his commandments alone, and to rise above the pull of visible things. In this way God takes pleasure in them, and the angels are zealous on their behalf. They gain love for one another and are made worthy of unfading blessings in the new and indestructible world.

If there are people who even now have not believed in Christ, or who have believed but do not keep his commandments, that is not his doing. For his part, the light of his knowledge is spread over everyone, and the table of his good things is set for everyone. That light and that table accuse those who have not believed, or who believed but did not act. Such a person is like one who stands under the sun and shuts his eyes so as not to see, or like one who is invited to the banquet and holds back his feet from going.

Chapter Five: Why these good things were not revealed until now.

Let us now go on to the question that is commonly asked: why did the coming of Christ not take place until this time, when it has been shown to be so beneficial to all rational beings? Was it perhaps because God did not know about it until now? Or did he know of it but lack the power to accomplish it? Or, having both, knowledge and power, did he resent our good like an evil being, and for that reason delay it until now? For whenever someone is the cause of delay in doing good, he is held back from doing it by ignorance, by weakness or by malice.

But that God knew from the beginning that he would raise up our Lord Christ is plain from the fact that he announced his coming beforehand, and announced the good things given to us through him, long ago to the patriarchs in his promises and through the prophets among the people of Israel. We cannot say that he does not know now that he will raise us from the dead merely because he has not already raised us. In the same way we cannot suppose that he did not know he would manifest our Lord Christ merely because he did not do this in deed from the beginning. Although he had not accomplished it in deed, he was announcing it, and its types were inscribed among the ancients.

If you like, let us also lift our eyes to the beginning of creation and examine it. Had he not been looking toward what was to come, he would not have created two heavens, which serve the order of the two worlds. And how can anyone think that he lacked the power? To renew us after we have come into being is not as hard as it was to bring us into being when we did not exist at all, when there was nothing from which we could be fashioned and receive our existence. And it is known that he is good. Had he been evil to begin with, he would never have changed to goodness, since God possesses everything that is his without change. Is this not an ineffable good? We could not come into being by our own will, yet he not only gave us existence, as he gave it to stones and wood, but raised us even above the dumb animals. He made us discerning and rational, and without grudging gave us authority over all visible things.

If, then, he was good from the beginning, and knowing, and powerful, nothing else prevented him from bringing all our good things into effect except our own weakness, which could not receive them all at once without training. In this the divine wisdom looked to what was best for us, and so his ineffable grace guided us accordingly. If one of us has a son or a pupil whom he wants to teach whatever craft he knows, does he not lead him from small things to great? If he wants to teach him [letters?], so to speak, he first teaches him the alphabet, then the combinations of letters and the syllables, so that he may learn them and spell them out. After these come psalms, through which he learns to read as well. When he has taught him to write correctly, until he has learned the shape of the script, then, after all this, he gives him books of commentary to read, so that he may grasp the meaning of the divine Scriptures. But if he forced the pupil to explain the meaning of words before he had learned to read, then plainly, since the pupil gains nothing, the teacher would also be shown to be out of his mind, striving to put on a roof before he has laid a foundation.

We are mortal and frail, yet we know how to manage our affairs in an orderly way. We do not deal with our sons and pupils according to our own knowledge and ability, but measure our teaching to them so that they are able to receive it. How much more fitting was it, then, for the Lord, who is wiser than all and better than all, to measure out everything in his providence for our benefit and according to our capacity, dealing with us not according to his own foreknowledge and power but according to our weakness.

Let us examine that ineffable wisdom, and see how from the beginning it led our nature step by step to perfect knowledge, like a compassionate father and a teacher who comes down to his pupils' level. Grace guided the first generations, from Adam to Noah, in a single order, like the first stage of children, for whom the alphabet is written out. It arranged everything that served both to frighten them and to urge them to keep away from evil and draw near to the practice of good. In the same way we too sometimes stir our children up, so as to bring them by every means to what is fitting, taking our cue from them as to whether we should deal with them this way or that.

So too God our Maker, who has always shown fatherly mercy to our race in his immeasurable grace, sometimes brought punishment on offenders. So it was with Adam and Eve at the very beginning, and with Cain, who killed his brother. When the report of this reached those who came after them, they would be terrified of turning to the practice of evil. We learn this from Lamech as well. When he killed a man unintentionally, he was seized with great fear, lamenting and mourning before his wives, as one who would receive punishment from God many times greater than Cain's. For he had killed after learning what evil sentence the murderer was handed over to.

At other times again he made the blood of the righteous Abel cry out from the ground after his death. By this he showed how much care God has for those who fear him: even after their death he hears their voice and avenges them on their oppressors. In this way he would urge everyone to strive to love his commandments and attend to them, as we see Enoch did. Enoch was so justified that he was even counted worthy to be taken away from among men, and of a dwelling that [human] nature had been given a small foretaste of in advance.

He brought the waters of the flood upon those first generations because of their wantonness, their wickedness and their evil deeds. He saved Noah and those with him, and gave them laws in which those before them had not been trained: that they might eat everything like green plants, after pouring out its blood, which in the dumb animals stands in place of a soul. So too we, once a child has learned the alphabet, write out for him the combinations of letters and the syllables, so that he may learn to spell.

Then again, after no short time, he chose Abraham, the head of the patriarchs. He gave him the law of circumcision and explicit promises concerning his descendants, something higher than what he gave the household of Noah. When his descendants had been tried by many evils in the land of Egypt, he brought them out from there with various mighty works and gave them diverse laws in writing. So too, once our sons and pupils have learned to spell, we write out psalms for them, so that they may also learn to read from them, and then we give them correct writing as well.

After our nature had in this way reached full stature, so to speak, and had passed through those first lessons and been trained in them, he brought about the coming of Christ. This teaches the perfection of knowledge and gives hope and the expectation of the good things to come. It is like someone who, after the lessons we have described, gives his son books of commentary to read, so that he may know the sense and meaning of what he learned before. Yet in all these generations he did not neglect to deal with the same matters as he had with the first generations. He brought punishment on the wicked and on sinners, made those of his household glorious and renowned, and arranged everything well for the sake of the goal we spoke of earlier.

Suppose someone has ten pupils who, as far as their instruction goes, stand at one stage, the alphabet. One of them neglects his lessons and goes out to play in the streets. Another sets about eating and drinking with no concern for his reading. Another yawns and falls asleep. Others again are wholly taken up with idle chatter about empty stories, and care nothing for the instruction they are given. The rest learn as they ought and value the study of their lessons above everything, as their master wishes. When the idle ones are called to recite and are punished, it is not because they did not learn to read and understand the meaning of the Scriptures. It is because they did not repeat the alphabet so as to say it as well as their fellows. In the same way, when God enters into judgment and examines people's deeds, he does not ask those of Adam's generation why they were not circumcised, nor those of Noah's household why they did not keep the Sabbath. Plainly he examines each generation in comparison with those who lived with it, repaying each person according to his works, in keeping with the time in which he lived and the laws from God that were given in his days.

And just as God does not require of the earlier generations what belongs to the later, since the later did not yet exist, so it was not fitting for nature to remain in one order without advancing. It would do a child no good to practise nothing but the alphabet until his old age. So the coming of Christ did no harm to those of old by not coming earlier, since they are not called to account for the way of life Christ taught. To us it has been of help beyond measure. It turned us from error to God, perfected us in complete knowledge, and promised us the good things to come, as I said above.

It is evident that it came at this time by great wisdom. Had it been shown earlier, the ancients could not have been capable of receiving it, just as someone who has only now begun learning to spell does not have the knowledge to grasp the meaning of books of commentary.

Someone may say that God could have fixed all knowledge in us without training, immediately, from the very beginning. Such a person is mistaken. Wanting to spare himself the labour, he places himself in the rank of the irrational creatures, which have everything they possess by nature, without training. Take again the chastity of turtledoves: for this reason we say that none of these species deserves either praise or blame, either a good reward or punishment. This would have been our case too, had we received that life, free from need and from wavering, without training and straight from our formation. That is why it was necessary for this present state to come first. The one who is being trained and taught must be led from small things to great.

"But," it is said, "he himself created us free to turn either way, and for that reason we sin. Why then does he judge us when we sin?" Who, then, is judged for being free to turn? Far from it: no one is. Freedom to turn and sin are not one and the same thing. By freedom to turn we mean that, when someone wishes to do something, he can incline equally toward either of two courses. By sin we mean the following. A person judges by his own discernment and has learned from God's commandments, or at least is able to judge and know that a thing is not fitting for him to do. Yet he neglects and overrides his discernment, scorns the divine commandments, and does the thing, whether for the sake of a moment's pleasure, out of spite against his fellow, or for any other reason. It is something he himself perceived, or could have perceived, ought not to be done, and the divine commandment had also forbidden him to do it. So God does not judge a person's freedom to turn toward what is not fitting. He judges the fact that the person did the deed although he could have restrained himself from doing it, and that, for whatever reason, he did not do what was fitting.

"But," it is said, "if he had not created us free to turn, we would not sin at all." Neither would we be justified at all. If he had created you such that you could not turn your back on God, you would have no sin. In the same way, if he had fashioned you such that you could not sin, you would have no righteousness at all. As it is, you can look equally toward either of them whenever you wish, so you have both sin and righteousness. You have sin because you could have pleased God, like the rest of humankind who in every generation pleased him and fulfilled his will, but you went after your desires and cared nothing for what is fitting. You have righteousness, again, because, being able to practise good, you honoured what is fitting and the fear of God above everything. For the one you are blamed and receive punishment; for the other you are praised and counted worthy to delight in the good things.

If we call dumb animals or sentient natures "free to turn", we use the term in a borrowed sense, meaning that they are variable in their nature. But when freedom to turn is said of rational beings, it is meant in the sense I gave above.

You may say that God could have done both for us: made us not free to turn from the very beginning, and also fixed in us the knowledge and discernment of everything fitting, without any experience of its opposite. Plainly whoever says this does not believe what he is saying, nor does he know what he is asking. Whatever comes into our minds as existing, in whatever way, we find to exist in one of the following modes. Apart from them nothing exists in any other way. Apart from them nothing exists in any other way, nor can it exist. There is God, the Maker of us all. There are all the rational beings, divided into two orders, the visible and the invisible. There are all the dumb animals. And there are natures without life and without sense. But God has no likeness, and never will.

How can a made thing be like its Maker, when it could not even give itself existence? How can a made thing be without beginning, when it has already come into being and did not exist before it came to be? Or how is it possible for one whose coming into being is bounded by time to have an unbounded nature? It is only of him whose nature nothing confines, neither time nor extension of any kind, that one can rightly conceive that he is prior to existence itself [?]. All these things belong to God alone: to bring all natures into being when they did not exist, while he himself exists in his own being and eternally, before all the ages and all the orders that rise up in thought. It belongs to him too that his nature is unbounded and unlimited, so that it cannot even be grasped. Along with all this comes the fact that he knows everything, though he has received nothing from anyone else and has gained no experience of anything. And it belongs to him to be as he is at all times, whenever anyone may think of him, receiving no change of any kind.

These, then, are God's own peculiar attributes, and no made being can attain to them. Wherever one of them is found, logic requires that all of them be found. It is therefore great audacity, the very insolence of Satan, for anyone to say that it would have been good if we had not been free to turn and not changeable, and had possessed all knowledge with full discernment from the very beginning. Such a person should recognize what rank he is seeking to stand in. Whatever punishment one might name, this would deserve it. Clearly whoever says it deserves even to be reduced to nothing.

If, then, it was not possible for us to be in such a rank, would we perhaps want to be like stones and wood and the four elements, and things of that kind, which do not incline toward sin? But if you put this question to any rational being at all, you will find them all alike refusing it. No one wishes to be even like the sun, which has no awareness of itself, though it shines brilliantly. It is clear that the sun has the nature of fire, since we can kindle fire from it in many ways if we wish. And it is clear that fire comes even out of stone. What is hidden within stones is plainly without life and without sensation, and no rational being would agree to that.

If not this, then perhaps we want to be like the dumb animals, to whom neither sin nor righteousness is reckoned, however they behave. We do not blame the cock, however much it may mate. Nor do we praise the turtledove for mating with only one. Nor do we say that the she-ass deserves punishment for conceiving from any male whatever. Nor do we call the mule blessed, which does not mate or conceive at all. So too with the rest of their kinds: we say they have neither sin nor righteousness in their actions. But all rational beings refuse this option too, just as they refused the first.

All these things were created for this reason. Besides supplying us with knowledge and with many uses, they teach us what blessedness the Creator of all has counted us worthy of, in not creating us like one of them. And so we may acknowledge the grace of his love toward our race. What then? If it is impossible to be like God, and we do not choose to be like one of the species of dumb animals or one of the insensible natures, what else can we say? Only that we should acknowledge God's grace in word and in deed, as far as we are able. He honoured us so greatly and raised us above all visible things. He also brought us near to himself and made us partakers in what is his, as was fitting.

Someone may ask why he did not create us like the angels. But they too are free to turn, just as we are. All the demons and the devil come from those orders. Yet it served our instruction that we human beings should be composed of the whole of creation, visible and invisible. In this way we would learn in our own person, and the angels likewise would learn through us, that there is one God, the Maker of all creatures visible and invisible. Had this not been so, it would have seemed that there were as many makers as there are different natures. But since the wise Maker gathered all the differences of creation into one living being, rational man, it is clearly known that, though natures differ and creatures vary, their Maker is one. He gathered them all and bound them together in one man, composed of all of them.

"But," it is said, "because we are free to turn, many sin, and for this reason they are handed over in Gehenna to unending punishment. What profit is it to them to have been rational and knowing, if they are not counted worthy of the heavenly good things?" Whoever says this ought to consider that those who sinned had the power not to sin, like the rest who pleased God, since they are of the very same nature. But because they despised and scorned the divine commandments of their own will, they are justly deprived of the heavenly blessings.

And yet even this, to be in Gehenna, is far higher and more excellent than to be without reason and without discernment. If my words are not believed, take someone who cannot enjoy the brilliant light of this sun that our senses perceive, and see which he would choose: to remain as he is, or to become an ass that has large eyes and sees keenly. "But," it may be said, "a blind man's defect is not so very bad." Then who is lower in this world than a leper [?]? Yet if you ask even him, you will find that he would rather remain in the pains he has than be changed into a camel, say, or anything else of the kind.

In the same way, those who go to Gehenna and fall into various punishments for their hateful deeds still receive their Maker's grace without fail. He did not reduce them to nothing, as they deserved, nor make them like dumb animals and insensible natures. That they are deprived of the ascent to heaven and of fellowship with the righteous, they put down to their own deeds. They are left without excuse, while even in this they praise the divine justice unceasingly.

There is also what I said above: that where there is knowledge of everything without experience of anything, and constancy in remaining always the same, without change in any form, all these must belong to God. Perhaps someone thinks this is false, "because," he says, "we believe that after the resurrection from the dead all rational beings receive perfect knowledge and remain unchanged without end." How far the one is from the other is clear to those who know how to listen. What I said was "knowledge of everything without experience of anything", and "constancy in remaining the same at whatever time one may think of". These are never found in us. We have already been tested in many things in this world and have undergone no small changes, so that not even in this way are we gods.

But however much one says on this subject, my honoured brother, it is never exhausted. Anyone who examines it carefully can see how briefly I have said all that is in this chapter.

Chapter Six: That it was necessary for some mediator to be taken, through whom we might receive these great good things from God.

Let us now show that it was not possible to receive these good things and inherit them without some mediation. Had anything been revealed from the beginning, we would not have profited from it, because our childishness and the reasons we have given would have prevented us from knowing it. In the same way, had God, the Lord of all, not acted at this time through some mediation, in keeping with his wisdom, their benefit would not have reached us. If God were visible, the mere sight of him would have been enough to instruct us. But since he is invisible, it is impossible to learn about him without some mediation.

It is said of the prophets that they saw the Lord, but plainly they did not see his nature. "For truth and grace," says John, "came through Jesus Christ." And what is the truth and the grace? He says: "No one has ever seen God." And as for him who dwells in light, plainly no human being has seen him or can see him, as the blessed Paul teaches in these words. So the ancients never saw God, nor will those who come later ever see him. I do not mean human beings only, but the invisible powers as well.

Everything that is visible is seen either in part or as a whole. We see the earth in part, and the heaven and the sea. Although we see only a part of each of them, because our sight cannot take in all four directions, we still say that we see the heaven, the earth and the sea. Small things, such as stones and wood and the like, we see whole and entire because they are small. God, then, cannot be seen in part, as the earth and the heaven are, because he is not composite and is not made up of parts. Nor again does he fall under sight like small things, because he is wholly uncircumscribed and unbounded.

If we sought to see him as he is, we would only be longing for our own destruction. Who would throw a little wax into a fiery furnace and find it again? Or who would cast a handful of dust into the great sea and be able to tell what had become of it? Among created works, all of them creatures, there are things that destroy and annihilate one another when they come near and fall upon each other. How much more, then, would this be so with God, the Maker of all, who is uncircumscribed in his divinity and ineffable in his glory! If our sight were to strike against him in his entirety, would we not be destroyed more surely than wax melts in fire, more surely than a little handful of dust is lost in many waters?

The great sea, because of its breadth and unfathomable depth, cannot be crossed by anyone without the mediation of a ship or a boat. [?] without some mediation, through which we might be guided to the knowledge of the Invisible One. The soul is created and circumscribed, yet because we do not see it, we cannot learn its will, or even that it exists, except through the action of one of the members of the body. How much more, then, with him who is the Maker of all and incomprehensible: we could not receive teaching about him or learn his will unless he revealed himself through one of his creatures.

Well, then, did God, who delights in good things, act in keeping with the abundant riches of his grace. He did not reveal himself to us without some mediation. He took from among us a perfect man for his revelation to us, and through him taught us perfect knowledge of himself and of his will, and promised us the heavenly good things that do not pass away.

Chapter Seven: That for these reasons our Lord God took nothing else at this time for his revelation but a man from among us

Let us now state the reasons why a man from among us was needed for the divine revelation at this time. People ask why God did not reveal himself to us by fire, or by a cloud, or by any other part of creation, as he did to the first fathers, but by a perfect man taken from our race. Our answer is that God did not reveal himself to us now by any of these parts because he had already revealed himself to our fathers by them. From the beginning God arranged the whole creation part by part, and then, when nothing was lacking, he gathered all of it at the end into one man, after whom he created nothing new. In the same way, after he had made himself known to our fathers part by part in the former generations, he now gathered all the parts of all his revelations, in the last times, in this man whom he took from us. After him he is not revealed again in anything else, for in him all the former things were brought to completion, and he endures forever, never to be undone. When God wished to bring about a partial salvation, to teach a teaching suited to the weak, and to supply well the need proper to each period of time, he completed his revelation to those he was teaching through a part of creation. But now that he wished to make a complete salvation shine out for all creation, and it pleased him to bring to perfection a teaching complete in every respect, he rightly took a man complete in body and soul as the bond of all creation, and in him all creatures, visible and invisible, are held together.

Again, Adam, the first man and the father of all people, obeyed the accuser from the very beginning of his formation and transgressed the divine commandment. He received from God the sentence of death, which spread out like a debt and was passed on to all his offspring. They added still more to the sentence of death that lay upon them through their various errors in the worship of idols and their defiling sins: they trampled on love for their neighbours, despised the honour owed to parents, and were blind even to the observances of the law of Moses. It was therefore necessary that a man, one of their own nature and their brother, should arise from the lineage of Adam, the first man. Being justified in all things and becoming blameless in all his conduct, he would lift the sentence of death from us, dissolve and abolish sin, deliver us from the slavery of Satan and the demons, free us from the curse of the law of Moses, and give us immortal life as our possession in the resurrection from the dead. For as death came through a man, so the resurrection of the dead also came through a man. As in Adam all people die, so in Christ all live. And as through the disobedience of one man many became sinners, so through the obedience of one man many become righteous. When someone incurs a debt and has nothing to repay it with, his property is taken from him and his offspring too are sold into slavery. But if someone arises from his line who is able by his diligence to repay his father's debts, he takes back the property and frees all his brothers from the bondage of sin and slavery. So too, after Adam became guilty of the debt by obeying the accuser, and he and all his offspring after him were enslaved to death, God took the man Jesus, the second Adam, from our race. In his goodness God made him blameless, and he died without guilt, for he had committed no sin at all, so that by his guiltlessness our debt might be cancelled. And since he was not enslaved to sin, he would bring us to life, we who because of sin had, as it were, received the sentence of death.

If God had been crucified and died, as the heretics say, no benefit at all would have come to us; rather he would have saved gods like himself. For if God is mortal, there are clearly many gods like him as well. But the true God shares in none of the sufferings of creatures. Someone might say that it shows greater mercy for him to die and for us to be saved, as when someone incurs a debt and another pays on behalf of those who have been enslaved and frees them. But this is exactly what the humanity of our Lord did. He alone was justified and became blameless, and he obtained immortal life for all people, who share his nature. It would have been easy for God, had it seemed good to him to help in that way, to bring us all to immortal life by a mere nod, without taking a man from among us. But he did not do this [?] of our Lord. He alone was justified and became blameless, and he obtained immortal life for all people, who share his nature. It would have been easy for God, had it seemed good to him to help in that way, to bring us all to immortal life by a mere nod, without taking a man from among us. But he did not do this, so that he would not be thought a lover of evil, as though he saved us while we remained in our sins, without anyone from among us having been justified. Instead, by taking a man from us and so freeing us from death and sin, he showed his justice and frightened us away from serving evil and wickedness, since the one who was not guilty gave himself up to death and in this way saved us. And since one alone was enough for him on behalf of our whole race, he made his unspeakable mercy shine out. All of us were obliged to become blameless before we could inherit immortal life, yet he granted this to us for the sake of one alone who was justified, so that we would not lose heart and give up the hope of being changed for the better.

These reasons, however, are stated with respect to the arrangements of the divine economy. For it is clear that from the very beginning it pleased God first to make our nature passible and mortal, and then at the end, after the training and testing of our rational nature in this world, to make us share in a life that is immortal and unchangeable. So that we might draw benefit from everything that concerns us, he presented death, which had been set in Adam's nature from his very formation, as though it had come upon us through sin. In this way we would all fear and dread transgressing the commandments of God, if disobedience is so evil that it even undoes the composition of a human being and separates the soul from the body. And that immortal life, which before the foundations of the world he had determined to decree for us at the appointed time, he made shine out through the man Jesus Christ, as the apostle Paul said: "For there is one mediator between God and humanity." He did this to draw all of us together and to urge us to love, and to teach us that righteousness has such power that, when it is found in one alone, it brings countless multitudes to life. This, then, was the divine will before all ages, and the arrangement of his economy benefited us in many ways, as I have said. Anyone who examines it and grasps the meaning of the Scriptures will rightly give the reasons that we are now setting out.

Above all, however, the assumption of our Lord's humanity was necessary for this reason: at this time, when our nature had reached, as one might say, its full stature, as I said, we needed to receive perfect teaching about God, who is known in three hypostases, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, equal in a nature without beginning and without limit. This could not have been revealed to rational beings through any part of creation. This is clear from the fact that, as long as God revealed himself to the ancients through such things, they lacked the knowledge to learn about that glorious nature of the Godhead which is known in three hypostases and is exalted above all composition, and above all limit and boundary in any place. Some of them supposed that his dwelling was in paradise; others confined his dwelling to heaven alone; and others thought that his activity was limited to Jerusalem. Nor did they allow any distinction of the hypostases of the Godhead.

We, however, have now learned through the man from among us that God is spirit and is in every place. Wherever one might think of, he is equally present there, and wherever he is, he is equally able to act in his very nature. That is, the whole world subsists in him, and he holds it like a grain of sand in the hand of one of us, and far more than words can say. We have learned too that this ineffable being exists in a threefold way in hypostases. From the fact that he was called Christ, we learn about the Father who anointed him and the Holy Spirit who filled him in place of the anointing oil: "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power." And again our Lord said of himself: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; for this reason he has anointed me." And from the fact that he is named Son, we contemplate the eternal Son who is with his Father, just as from this bread, which is named the body of Christ, we are led up to that body which is in heaven. None of those parts of creation through which God was revealed to the ancients, such as the fire and the cloud, the stones and timbers of the temple, the tabernacle and the golden plate, could be called by the name of Son. But when the man of our Lord was called Son of God, it did not seem a novelty, since many had been called this, as in "I have begotten and raised up sons," and "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High." Yet when people came to him and saw his works, which were beyond his nature, and heard him say, "I and my Father are one," and "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father," they came to understand that the eternal Son from the Father was hidden in him, who did these things through him and to whom such words belong.

If you beckon with your hand, nod your head or wink with your eyes, the soul, hidden in the body and invisible, makes known some small thing: that someone should go or come, stand or sit, or something of that kind. But all its wishes and the knowledge of its thoughts it teaches and brings into the open through the tongue alone. In the same way, when the invisible God was revealed to the ancients through one of these parts of creation, he taught them a partial knowledge suited to the need their weakness required. But now that he has taken a perfect man from among us, he has taught us all his wishes through him and made us know his being perfectly, as far as was possible, like the soul that reveals all its knowledge and brings it into the open through the tongue. So for this reason too it was necessary that a man from among us be assumed.

Again, the resurrection from the dead was to be given to us as our possession, and the promise of ascension to heaven had been made. We would not have believed that any of these things would be fulfilled for us had we not seen someone from among us, sharing our nature as we do, who died, rose and ascended to heaven first. But since these things were first carried out in one like us, we believe that it is not difficult for them to be accomplished in us as well through him, since we are of his nature. For he who already received them in deed [?] and to the ascension of the righteous to heaven.

Again, it is through him that God will judge all people, as the apostle said: "when God judges the secrets of people according to my gospel through Jesus Christ." The righteous feel the delight of good things more keenly, and the wicked the bitterness of the punishment they receive, when they receive the reward for all their deeds from one who is visible like themselves. Further, after the resurrection from the dead and the ascension of the righteous to heaven, they will not build buildings of hewn stone, timber, cedar and fine stones in which to worship God, as in this world. Instead he will take the place of the temple for them, and in him they will worship the holy Trinity without ceasing. They will show their love for God by offering him, in this man as in a rational temple, the worship they owe him, together with praise and thanksgiving. In him they will have consolation and rest, and their mind, which longs to see God, will find rest in him as in a calm harbour. Seeing him, they see as it were that other one, and from him they are lifted up to the invisible one, as from an image to its original. For he is "the image of the invisible God." If we ourselves, when someone dear to us is far away, are comforted by gazing at his image, how much more will the righteous be consoled and rejoice? The burning flame of love in their mind, which is eager to see God their creator and the cause of all their good things, will find satisfaction in this rational image, which is clothed in divine glory, exalted above all, and rules over all creatures. In him they see, as it were, the one who is invisible to them; in him they contemplate the one hidden in his being, and they find satisfaction concerning him.

All these reasons required that a man from among us be assumed, O our honoured brother: the gathering and fulfilment of all former things; the salvation of all creatures visible and invisible; the undoing of all the afflictions that, through Adam the first man, appeared to have gained possession of our nature; the condemnation of Satan [?] receives according to the justice of his deeds; and in him the righteous show their love for God, and in him they find satisfaction for the invisibility of their maker and benefactor.

Chapter Eight: That Christ our Lord is not a mere man

Let us now resolve a difficulty raised by many. When they hear us set out the distinctive features of our Lord's humanity and the reasons why it was assumed, they attack us, saying, "So according to your account he is a mere man, and he alone was enough to save." They say this out of ignorance and lack of understanding. If they looked carefully at what has been said, they would understand our meaning: that in him God the Word is revealed with his Father and the Holy Spirit; that in him, as in a rational temple, God is worshipped without ceasing; and that in him again, as in an image, God is seen by all his righteous ones. These things do not allow the man of our Lord to be considered a mere man, and they alone, once stated, are enough to show his greatness and his distinction from all creatures. Still, let us give other reasons too which show that God was in the man assumed from among us.

We said above that he had to be perfectly justified and blameless in everything, in thoughts, words and deeds [?] and God extended help to him toward the excellence of his will. He was "justified in the Spirit." And since, once he had fulfilled the law of Moses, its course had to come to an end, as something now completed by him, God had to be in him for this reason too. For it belonged to God alone to abolish the law, as the one who had also given it in the beginning. Again, once the law had ceased from its course and the way of life of the new covenant was beginning, it was necessary that people receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, which makes sons of those who become God's household through faith in him. For this reason too we say that God dwelt in him, since God alone was able to give the grace of the Spirit. Moreover, the man of our Lord could not have risen from the dead and ascended to heaven if God had not been in him. For it was God alone who could grant [?] the undoing of death. Nor could we at the end receive new life, nor the righteous be raised to the heights above, if he had been a mere man. For all these reasons, then, it was necessary that God should also be in the man assumed from the seed of the house of David, just as it was for the earlier reasons we have given. It was not possible that not [?]

Chapter Nine: Why the man of our Lord was not taken from the earth, but from a virgin without union with a man

It has now been shown that we are gathered today because of the good things given to us through our Lord Christ. It has also become known what these good things are, and it has been revealed that what was not revealed before time was arranged with great wisdom for our benefit. It has further become clear that something had to act as mediator through which these good things would reach us, and that this was nothing other than a man: not a mere man, but one in whom God, almighty and all-powerful, was also present. Let us now say why God did not take the man of our Lord from the earth, as he did the first Adam, and why he was born of a woman without union with a man. When we have shown this, let us turn to why God arranged that he be conceived in the season of Nisan, and what we can learn from the fact that he was born at this season. We will add a little exhortation, so as to give the whole subject its completion, as I said at the beginning.

From the very beginning of our formation we have been provoking God, transgressing the divine commandments and trampling on the free choice of our discernment, because of our inclination toward [?]. In every generation we have plainly shown ourselves opposed to God in our words and our deeds, so that even if we were reduced to nothing, we would deserve it [?] apart from a few who were found among us in various generations, like pearls in the sand. If God had taken the man of our Lord from the earth, as he did the first Adam, we would all have been cut off from hope from then on. We would have supposed that God had rejected our race because of our sins, and we would no longer have any hope of something better. Therefore God, whose mercy and fatherly goodness toward our race from the beginning are beyond measure, saw fit to take him not from the earth but from our own nature. In this way he would teach us that the immortal, impassible and incorruptible life which our Lord received in his resurrection from the dead passes to our whole race, and that all of us together share in it, because he is of our nature and not a stranger to us. Because we share the nature of the first Adam, all the afflictions the first man received passed to us and spread over us all. In the same way, because our Lord too is of our nature, and he became the beginning of the good things to come, as Adam was of the afflictions we have spoken of, we believe and hope that we will all share in immortal and impassible life with our Lord Christ, just as we shared with the first Adam in these things here, which are full of every distress. As through Adam we all die, so through Christ we all live [?] like the first Adam, or from some other source, wherever one might suggest.

It is clear that although he was conceived and born of the virgin Mary without union, he shares in the whole nature of men and of women, and something of them all is in him. For the blessed Mary too, like all women, came from a man and a woman. And if she who bore him was constituted from both kinds, men and women, then necessarily there is in him too something of them all, since he was born of one constituted from both. For this reason the Scriptures call him son of David and of Abraham, since the blessed Mary, from whom he was born, was descended from their seed. Therefore the good things that are in him also pass to all people, to men and women alike, since he is akin to all in nature, as I said.

He was conceived of the Holy Spirit without union with a man so that it might be known that he is the beginning of the new economy and of the world to come, like Adam, who was formed from the earth without union and became head and father of this world. The one who was to be head and beginning of the mortal way of life was fittingly created from lifeless earth. But this one, who became the beginning and revealer of this world [?] immortal life, was taken from a living earth, the virgin Mary, without union with a man. The newness of his formation without seed was enough to proclaim that he was the beginning of the new economy, which grants the resurrection of the dead that comes about by the power of the Spirit, the Spirit which was not too weak to form him from a virgin without union, beyond the order of nature.

Chapter Ten: Why God arranged that he be conceived in the first season

God arranged that he be conceived in the season of Nisan because it was in this very season that God made the whole creation. The nature of the season taught that the one who created in the beginning is the very same who now renews all things through the one who was conceived. He was then born at this season according to the order of nature which God had established from the very beginning. From the correspondence and likeness of events we say this: at this season the portion of daylight has shrunk and gone down to nine hours, and from then on the day begins to win back its power of light from the night's grip of darkness. Again, today there is no fruit among us, either of crops or of trees: the seed is only beginning to sprout, and all the trees have shed even their leaves. In the same way both of these things were seen among all people [?] the coming of our Lord Christ. The light of the knowledge of truth was being extinguished from our souls, and the darkness of the error of idol worship gripped our minds, while we were stripped and despoiled of all the fruits of the works of righteousness. But our Lord and Saviour Christ came and shone in our mind. He drove from us the darkness of the worship of things made by hands and guided us to the perfect knowledge of the holy Trinity, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. He also gave us the grace of the Spirit, by which we are enabled to bear and produce the fruits of righteousness that please God our maker.

The pagans, who worship the elements, hold a great feast every year on this day everywhere, on the grounds that the sun begins to prevail and take hold of its power in greater measure. They ought to be ashamed. If it is truly a fit occasion for joy and a great feast that from then on the day begins to take from the night, then, the two being equal, it is just as fitting that at another season the darkness of night begins to take from the day the power of the sun. If the night kept lengthening and did not turn back and shorten, human life would perish. In the same way, if the day, once it began to lengthen, did not shorten again, this world could not continue. Without summer and winter, heat and cold, our way of life could not be sustained by the produce of our crops, so that they may be completed [?] these things, which could not exist without the rising and setting of the sun and the lengthening and shortening of night and day. So the benefit we have when the sun prevails is the very same we have when it wanes. They should either hold the feasts of pagan error at both changes or at neither, since the benefit of both is equal, and it comes from God, who ordered them so.

Chapter Eleven: Exhortation on good conduct

So they, as I said, held a feast for the sun, on the grounds that at this season it begins to overcome the grip of darkness, though it turns back and wanes again. But the holy Church celebrates the feast of the birth of Christ, the Sun of righteousness, who has begun to overcome error and Satan and never wanes again. Rather, the further he advances, the more his power takes hold, until all rational beings, visible and invisible, are made subject to his authority. "To him every knee shall bow, in heaven, on earth and under the earth." And just as our feasts are greater and stronger than those of the pagans, since the truth of knowledge is found with us alone, so it is fitting that our conduct in the fear of God be finer and purer than that of the rest of humanity. We should take care of both alike: the reading of the Scriptures and their interpretation, the teaching about the feasts and their reasons, and also the excellent conduct that pleases Christ our Lord. And we should care for our companions and our brothers more than for ourselves, if indeed we are disciples of the apostles who modelled themselves on their Lord [?].

For all of them gave up everything for our benefit. They laboured night and day, in summer and winter, on sea and on land, by every means and in every way, so that all of us might draw near to the household of our Lord Christ and find the good things prepared in heaven for those who believe rightly and live properly. They despised every evil and gave their lives to death for us, because our life in Christ was more precious to them than their own life in this world. And why do I say "in this world"? For one of them even chose to be estranged from the good things to come for the sake of all his brothers, so that they might share in the good things of Christ. He says, "I could pray that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers and my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are the children of Israel." If, then, the blessed Paul asked in prayer for his own ruin and very nearly his destruction for the benefit of the community, how can we not be ashamed and embarrassed, and fall into great fear and trembling, when we call ourselves their disciples and yet do not model ourselves [?] on their conduct and their perfect intentions? Let us rather be like the apostles our teachers in everything, as far as possible, so that we may share with them in the heavenly good things. However fervent we may be in their teaching, and however much we confess their faith, if their conduct is not found in us we will not reach the place where they are going. We become instead like the blind, on whom the sun's rays are spread but who do not enjoy their brightness, because they have no organs to receive their effect. Truly, good conduct is the demonstration of right faith and the confirmation of perfect teaching, without which [?] that our teaching is not believed by outsiders either. And we who are inside are not thought to have learned the [?] of the fear of God. Let us rather take care for our conduct and for love toward one another. Let us not be a cause of evil for ourselves and a stumbling block to all who see us, but let us prepare ourselves for good works, so that we may be worthy of the voice that says, "Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom that was prepared for you before the foundation of the world," together with all the righteous ones of Christ. To him be glory, and may his mercies be upon us for ever. Amen.
Here ends the Cause of the Nativity, composed by Mar
Thomas, the teacher of Edessa. May his prayer be
upon the sinner who wrote this. Amen.
